```{python}
#| label: setup
import os
import pandas as pd
import altair as alt
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

```

## Methods

### Data acquisition

The original tab-delimited file is downloaded and saved unchanged in
`data/raw/AmesHousing.txt`. A CSV copy is created for the existing analysis.
This step changes the file format without cleaning or filtering the data.

```{python}
#| label: load-raw

from io import BytesIO
import requests

url = "https://jse.amstat.org/v19n3/decock/AmesHousing.txt"

# Keep the existing CSV path.
data = "../data/raw/AmesHousing.csv"
txt_path = "../data/raw/AmesHousing.txt"

# Download the original data.
response = requests.get(url, timeout=30)
response.raise_for_status()

# Preserve text values during format conversion, including leading zeros,
# empty fields, and literal NA labels.
csv_copy = pd.read_csv(
    BytesIO(response.content),
    sep="\t",
    encoding="utf-8-sig",
    dtype=str,
    keep_default_na=False,
)

required_columns = {
    "Gr Liv Area", "Overall Qual", "Year Built", "SalePrice"
}

if (
    csv_copy.shape != (2930, 82)
    or not required_columns.issubset(csv_copy.columns)
):
    raise ValueError("Unexpected Ames Housing data format or dimensions.")

os.makedirs("../data/raw", exist_ok=True)

# Save the original download without changing its contents.
with open(txt_path, "wb") as output:
    output.write(response.content)

# Create the CSV copy used by the existing analysis.
csv_copy.to_csv(data, index=False, encoding="utf-8")

# Keep the existing loading step and variable name.
raw = pd.read_csv(data)

raw.shape
```

### Cleaning

We keep the target (sale price) and the three features in our question,
living area, overall quality, and house age. We give them more readable and
consistent names. Instead of the year a house was built, we use its age,
calculated as the reference year (2026) minus the year built, so that the
feature is a number of years. The cleaned data is saved as a csv.

```{python}
#| label: clean-data
cleaned = raw[["Gr Liv Area", "Overall Qual", "SalePrice"]].copy()
cleaned.columns = ["living_area", "overall_quality", "sale_price"]
cleaned["house_age"] = 2026 - raw["Year Built"]

os.makedirs("../data/processed", exist_ok=True)
cleaned.to_csv("../data/processed/ames_cleaned.csv", index=False)
```


### Training and Testing Data

We are separating the train and test data with 80: 20 ratio. We are doing this
before any exploratory analysis so the test set cannot influence our decisions
and there is no leakage.

```{python}
#| label: split-data
train_df, test_df = train_test_split(
    cleaned, test_size=0.2, random_state= 552
)

train_df.to_csv("../data/processed/ames_train.csv", index=False)
test_df.to_csv("../data/processed/ames_test.csv", index=False)

```



### Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
```{python}
#| label: tbl-eda-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary statistics of the training data, with each feature's correlation with sale price."
labels = {
    "living_area": "Living area (sq ft)",
    "house_age": "House age in 2026 (years)",
    "overall_quality": "Overall quality (1-10)",
    "sale_price": "Sale price (US$)",
}
features = ["living_area", "house_age", "overall_quality"]

summary = (
    train_df[features + ["sale_price"]]
    .describe()
    .T[["count", "mean", "std", "min", "50%", "max"]]
    .rename(columns={"50%": "median"})
)
summary["corr. with price"] = train_df.corr()["sale_price"]
summary.loc["sale_price", "corr. with price"] = None
summary = summary.rename(index=labels).round(2)
summary
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-eda
#| fig-cap: "Sale price against each feature in the training data. Points are semi-transparent to show overlap; the red line is a linear trend."
points_area = alt.Chart(train_df).mark_circle(opacity=0.25).encode(
    x=alt.X("living_area", title="Living area (sq ft)"),
    y=alt.Y("sale_price", title="Sale price (US$)"),
)
line_area = points_area.transform_regression("living_area", "sale_price").mark_line(color="red")
chart_area = points_area + line_area

points_age = alt.Chart(train_df).mark_circle(opacity=0.25).encode(
    x=alt.X("house_age", title="House age in 2026 (years)"),
    y=alt.Y("sale_price", title="Sale price (US$)"),
)
line_age = points_age.transform_regression("house_age", "sale_price").mark_line(color="red")
chart_age = points_age + line_age

points_quality = alt.Chart(train_df).mark_circle(opacity=0.25).encode(
    x=alt.X("overall_quality", title="Overall quality (1-10)"),
    y=alt.Y("sale_price", title="Sale price (US$)"),
)
line_quality = points_quality.transform_regression("overall_quality", "sale_price").mark_line(color="red")
chart_quality = points_quality + line_quality

chart_area | chart_age | chart_quality
```

### Processing pipeline and baseline

We use living area, house age, and overall quality as numeric predictors.
Median imputation is included in the preprocessing pipeline to handle missing
predictor values. Predictors are retained in their original units.

We evaluate a mean-prediction baseline using five-fold cross-validation within
the training set. In each fold, the baseline predicts the mean sale price of
that fold's training observations. Performance is summarized using root mean
squared error (RMSE), measured in US dollars, and R-squared.

```{python}
#| label: preprocessing-baseline

from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

numeric_features = ["living_area", "house_age", "overall_quality"]

X_train = train_df[numeric_features]
y_train = train_df["sale_price"]

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric_features)
    ],
    remainder="drop",
)

dummy_pipeline = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        ("preprocessor", preprocessor),
        ("regressor", DummyRegressor(strategy="mean")),
    ]
)

cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=552)

cv_results = cross_validate(
    dummy_pipeline,
    X_train,
    y_train,
    cv=cv,
    scoring={
        "rmse": "neg_root_mean_squared_error",
        "r2": "r2",
    },
    error_score="raise",
)

# Convert scikit-learn's negative RMSE scores back to positive errors.
fold_scores = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "RMSE (US$)": -cv_results["test_rmse"],
        "R-squared": cv_results["test_r2"],
    }
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-dummy-baseline
#| tbl-cap: "Mean and standard deviation of the dummy baseline scores across five cross-validation folds."

baseline_summary = (
    fold_scores
    .agg(["mean", "std"])
    .rename(index={"mean": "CV mean", "std": "CV standard deviation"})
    .round(4)
)

baseline_summary
```

The negative R^2 in the baseline is normal, because every single fold uses the average sale price within each fold. This will be different for the validation. We can use the same five fold to compare it with the linear regression model later on.


### Main model

We fit a multiple linear regression model using the same predictors,
preprocessing pipeline, and five cross-validation folds as the dummy baseline.
The test set is reserved for the final evaluation.

```{python}
#| label: linear-model-cv

from pathlib import Path
from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, root_mean_squared_error

linear_pipeline = clone(dummy_pipeline).set_params(
    regressor=LinearRegression()
)

linear_cv_results = cross_validate(
    linear_pipeline,
    X_train,
    y_train,
    cv=cv,
    scoring={
        "rmse": "neg_root_mean_squared_error",
        "r2": "r2",
    },
    error_score="raise",
)

linear_fold_scores = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "RMSE (US$)": -linear_cv_results["test_rmse"],
        "R-squared": linear_cv_results["test_r2"],
    }
)

linear_cv_results

linear_fold_scores
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-model-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Mean performance and standard deviation across the same five training-set cross-validation folds."

model_cv_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        model_name: {
            "CV RMSE (US$)": scores["RMSE (US$)"].mean(),
            "RMSE SD (US$)": scores["RMSE (US$)"].std(),
            "CV R-squared": scores["R-squared"].mean(),
            "R-squared SD": scores["R-squared"].std(),
        }
        for model_name, scores in {
            "Dummy (mean)": fold_scores,
            "Multiple linear regression": linear_fold_scores,
        }.items()
    }
).T

model_cv_summary.round(
    {
        "CV RMSE (US$)": 2,
        "RMSE SD (US$)": 2,
        "CV R-squared": 4,
        "R-squared SD": 4,
    }
)
```

We fit the specified pipeline on the full training set and evaluate it once
on the held-out test set. Test performance is not used to select features
or tune the model.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-linear-model-test
#| tbl-cap: "Final held-out test performance of the multiple linear regression model."

linear_pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

X_test = test_df[numeric_features]
y_test = test_df["sale_price"]

linear_test_predictions = linear_pipeline.predict(X_test)

linear_test_metrics = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Model": ["Multiple linear regression"],
        "Training observations": [len(y_train)],
        "Test observations": [len(y_test)],
        "Test RMSE (US$)": [
            root_mean_squared_error(y_test, linear_test_predictions)
        ],
        "Test R-squared": [
            r2_score(y_test, linear_test_predictions)
        ],
    }
).set_index("Model")

linear_test_metrics.round(
    {
        "Test RMSE (US$)": 2,
        "Test R-squared": 4,
    }
)
```
